definition.text: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that connects a research idea to observable evidence.

anchor.quote: A hypothesis is a testable prediction about how the world will behave if our idea is correct

facts.text: A strong hypothesis is specific enough that evidence could support or challenge it.

anchor.quote: As specific hypotheses are tested, theories are modified and refined

facts.text: A hypothesis bridges abstract theory and the real-world observations that can test it.

anchor.quote: it bridges the gap between the realm of ideas and the real world

misconceptions.text: Students treat a hypothesis as a topic or opinion rather than a testable prediction.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask what observable result would count as evidence against the prediction.

examples.text: If retrieval practice improves retention, then students who use weekly practice quizzes should remember more concepts two weeks later.

mcBank.stem: Which statement is a research hypothesis?
options: If feedback is immediate, then revision quality will improve
Feedback is important in writing courses

mapping.claim: the predicted relationship in the hypothesis
mapping.evidence: observable results that could support or challenge the prediction

attribution: OpenStax Psychology 2e, §2.1 Why Is Research Important?

definition.text: An operational definition specifies the concrete actions or measures used to observe a variable.

anchor.quote: description of what actions and operations will be used to measure the dependent variables and manipulate the independent variables

facts.text: Operational definitions let others understand exactly how and what a researcher measured.

anchor.quote: allowing others to understand exactly how and what a researcher measures

facts.text: A weak operational definition can make a construct look measurable while hiding what was actually counted.

anchor.quote: An operational definition is a precise description of our variables

misconceptions.text: Students define a construct with another abstract word instead of naming the observation or measure.
misconceptions.corrective: Replace the abstraction with a concrete instrument, behavior, score, or coding rule.

examples.text: Instead of defining engagement as 'interest,' measure engagement as voluntary discussion posts submitted before the deadline.

mcBank.stem: A study says anxiety means a score above 10 on a validated short anxiety scale. This is a

mapping.measure: the concrete action, instrument, or score used to observe it
mapping.what the measure captures: the part of the construct visible through the chosen method
mapping.what it misses: construct meaning not captured by that measurement choice

attribution: OpenStax Psychology 2e, Ch. 2 Key Terms and §2.3

definition.text: The independent variable is manipulated or controlled; the dependent variable is the measured outcome.

anchor.quote: An independent variable is manipulated or controlled by the experimenter

facts.text: In a well-designed experiment, the independent variable should be the key difference between experimental and control groups.

anchor.quote: the independent variable is the only important difference between the experimental and control groups

facts.text: The dependent variable is what the researcher measures to estimate the effect of the manipulation.

anchor.quote: A dependent variable is what the researcher measures to see how much effect the independent variable had

misconceptions.text: Students reverse the variables because the outcome feels more important than the manipulation.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask what the researcher changes or compares first; that is the independent variable.

examples.text: If note-taking format is varied to test exam performance, note-taking format is the independent variable and exam score is the dependent variable.

mcBank.stem: A researcher changes the amount of sleep participants get and measures reaction time. Reaction time is the

mapping.measure: the independent-variable condition and dependent-variable outcome
mapping.what the measure captures: the observed effect of the manipulation on the outcome
mapping.what it misses: other differences between groups that the design did not control

definition.text: Correlation describes a relationship between variables, but it does not by itself demonstrate cause and effect.

anchor.quote: Correlations do not tell us anything about causation

facts.text: A confounding variable can produce an apparent relationship between the variables of interest.

anchor.quote: some other factor, a confounding variable, is actually causing the systematic movement in our variables of interest

facts.text: Experiments are the standard way to demonstrate causation because they manipulate a variable and compare outcomes.

anchor.quote: the only way to demonstrate causation is by conducting an experiment

misconceptions.text: Students infer cause from a strong relationship without checking for confounds or design limits.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask whether the study manipulated the cause and ruled out plausible alternative explanations.

examples.text: Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer; heat is a confound, not evidence that ice cream causes drowning.

mcBank.stem: A correlation between study app use and higher grades does not prove the app caused the grades because
options: a confounding variable may explain the relationship

mapping.proposed cause: the variable being treated as causal
mapping.alternative explanation: a confounding variable or design limitation

definition.text: Informed consent tells participants what to expect, including risks, and makes participation voluntary.

anchor.quote: An informed consent form provides a written description of what participants can expect during the experiment

facts.text: Participants should be told that involvement is voluntary and can stop without penalty.

anchor.quote: their involvement is completely voluntary and can be discontinued without penalty at any time

facts.text: Institutional Review Boards review human-participant experiments before approval.

anchor.quote: An institution's IRB requires several components in any experiment it approves

misconceptions.text: Students treat consent as a signature only, ignoring comprehension, voluntariness, and withdrawal rights.
misconceptions.corrective: Check whether the participant understands the study, risks, voluntary status, and right to stop.

examples.text: A survey consent page states the topic, time required, potential discomfort, data use, voluntary nature, and how to withdraw.

mcBank.stem: Which consent statement is ethically strongest?
options: You may stop participating at any time without penalty
You must complete every item after starting
The researcher will explain risks after data collection
Participation is required for course credit

mapping.maker and context: the research procedure and consent context
mapping.what it can support: claims gathered under ethical participation conditions
